title: House Price Prediction
aim: Predict house prices using area, bedrooms, bathrooms, age and location features.
data: 800 generated houses. Area: square feet; age: years; price: INR lakh. Location has three categories.
theory: Linear regression estimates coefficients by minimizing squared residuals. Categorical locations are one-hot encoded; numerical features are imputed and scaled using training data only.
code:
n = 800
X = pd.DataFrame({'area': rng.uniform(500, 3500, n),
    'bedrooms': rng.integers(1, 6, n),
    'bathrooms': rng.integers(1, 5, n),
    'age': rng.integers(0, 41, n),
    'location': rng.choice(['central', 'suburb', 'outskirts'], n)})
premium = X.location.map({'central': 30, 'suburb': 15, 'outskirts': 0})
y = (0.035*X.area + 5*X.bedrooms + 4*X.bathrooms
     - 0.5*X.age + premium + rng.normal(0, 7, n))
model = make_pipeline(tabular_preprocessor(X), LinearRegression())
metrics = evaluate(model, X, y, '01_house_prices', classification=False)
limitation: Generated prices follow a near-linear rule; the score does not establish performance on real property transactions.
conclusion: Measured results: MAE = 5.9756; RMSE = 7.4847; R2 = 0.9565; baseline_MAE = 29.8094. Generated prices follow a near-linear rule; the score does not establish performance on real property transactions.

title: Loan Approval Prediction
aim: Predict approval from income, credit history, loan amount and employment information.
data: 1,000 generated applications. Income and loan amount are in INR lakh; credit history is a binary indicator.
theory: Logistic regression maps a linear score to a probability using the sigmoid function. A stratified split preserves label proportions; scaling and employment encoding are fitted only on training rows.
code:
n = 1000
X = pd.DataFrame({'income': rng.uniform(3, 30, n),
    'credit_history': rng.binomial(1, 0.75, n),
    'loan_amount': rng.uniform(2, 60, n),
    'employment': rng.choice(['salaried', 'self_employed', 'unemployed'], n)})
job = X.employment.map({'salaried': 0.8, 'self_employed': 0.2, 'unemployed': -1})
score = 0.13*X.income + 2*X.credit_history - 0.07*X.loan_amount + job - 1.5
y = rng.binomial(1, 1/(1 + np.exp(-score)))
print('Labels: 0 = rejected; 1 = approved')
model = make_pipeline(tabular_preprocessor(X),
                      LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, random_state=SEED))
metrics = evaluate(model, X, y, '02_loan_approval')
limitation: The labels are simulated for teaching. Real lending requires representative data, policy checks and fairness evaluation.

title: Employee Promotion Prediction
aim: Predict promotion using experience, performance rating, training score and prior achievements.
data: 900 generated employee records with simulated promotion labels.
theory: A decision tree recursively partitions the feature space using impurity reduction. Limiting tree depth and minimum leaf size reduces overfitting.

    'performance_rating': rng.integers(1, 6, n),
    'training_score': rng.uniform(30, 100, n),
    'previous_achievements': rng.integers(0, 5, n)})

         + 0.35*X.previous_achievements + 0.05*X.experience - 1.8)

                               random_state=SEED)
metrics = evaluate(model, X, y, '04_employee_promotion')

title: Customer Churn Prediction
aim: Identify customers likely to leave a telecom service using usage, contracts, payment method and monthly charges.
data: 1,200 generated telecom customers; usage in GB, tenure in months, and monthly charges in currency units.
theory: A random forest averages multiple trees trained on bootstrap samples with randomized feature selection. Class weighting accounts for unequal label frequencies.
code:
n = 1200
X = pd.DataFrame({'usage_gb': rng.uniform(1, 100, n),
    'tenure_months': rng.integers(1, 73, n),
    'contract': rng.choice(['monthly', 'annual', 'two_year'], n),
    'payment_method': rng.choice(['automatic', 'manual'], n),
    'monthly_charges': rng.uniform(20, 120, n)})
score = (1.4*(X.contract=='monthly') + 0.5*(X.payment_method=='manual')
         + 0.025*X.monthly_charges - 0.045*X.tenure_months
         + 0.005*X.usage_gb - 2)
y = rng.binomial(1, 1/(1 + np.exp(-score)))
print('Labels: 0 = retained; 1 = churned')
model = make_pipeline(tabular_preprocessor(X), RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=150, max_depth=8, min_samples_leaf=5,
    class_weight='balanced', random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1))
metrics = evaluate(model, X, y, '05_customer_churn')
limitation: The generated churn probabilities are noisy. Recall for the churn class matters more than accuracy alone for retention planning.

title: Customer Segmentation
aim: Group customers by age, annual income and spending score without predefined labels.
data: 450 generated customers from three overlapping profiles. Income is in thousands of currency units; spending score ranges from 1 to 100.
theory: K-Means minimizes within-cluster squared distance. Features are standardized, candidate values of k are compared by silhouette score, and centres are converted back to original units for interpretation.
code:
centres = [[25, 35, 75], [45, 90, 65], [55, 50, 25]]
parts = [rng.normal(c, [8, 15, 14], size=(150, 3)) for c in centres]
X = pd.DataFrame(np.vstack(parts), columns=['age', 'annual_income', 'spending_score'])
X['age'] = X.age.clip(18, 80)
X['annual_income'] = X.annual_income.clip(10, 160)
X['spending_score'] = X.spending_score.clip(1, 100)
scaler = StandardScaler()
Z = scaler.fit_transform(X)
candidates = {}
for k in range(2, 7):
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=SEED).fit(Z)
    candidates[k] = (silhouette_score(Z, km.labels_), km)
best_k = max(candidates, key=lambda k: candidates[k][0])
score, model = candidates[best_k]
print('Silhouette by k:', {k: round(v[0], 3) for k, v in candidates.items()})
print('Selected k:', best_k)
print('Cluster sizes:', np.bincount(model.labels_))
print('Centres in original units:')
print(pd.DataFrame(scaler.inverse_transform(model.cluster_centers_),
                   columns=X.columns).round(2).to_string(index=False))
plt.scatter(X.annual_income, X.spending_score, c=model.labels_, cmap='viridis', s=18)
plt.xlabel('Annual income (thousands)'); plt.ylabel('Spending score')
plt.title('Customer segments; age also used for clustering')
plot_save('08_customer_segments')
metrics = {'selected_k': best_k, 'silhouette': score}
limitation: Silhouette is an internal measure computed on the same data used for clustering. Cluster numbers are arbitrary, not externally verified customer categories.

title: Used Car Price Prediction
aim: Predict used-car prices from age, kilometres driven, engine capacity, fuel type and transmission.
data: 1,000 generated cars. Price: INR lakh; distance: kilometres; engine: cubic centimetres.
theory: Random forest regression averages decision-tree predictions and can represent nonlinear relationships. Fuel and transmission are encoded inside the training pipeline.
code:
n = 1000
X = pd.DataFrame({'age': rng.uniform(0, 15, n),
    'kilometers_driven': rng.uniform(1000, 200000, n),
    'engine_capacity': rng.choice([1000, 1200, 1500, 2000, 2500], n),
    'fuel_type': rng.choice(['petrol', 'diesel', 'electric'], n),
    'transmission': rng.choice(['manual', 'automatic'], n)})
y = (2 + 0.006*X.engine_capacity*np.exp(-0.08*X.age)
     - 0.000012*X.kilometers_driven + 1.5*(X.transmission=='automatic')
     + 2*(X.fuel_type=='electric') + rng.normal(0, 0.6, n)).clip(0.5)
model = make_pipeline(tabular_preprocessor(X), RandomForestRegressor(
    n_estimators=150, min_samples_leaf=2, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1))
metrics = evaluate(model, X, y, '09_used_car_prices', classification=False)
limitation: The generated price rule omits brand, condition, accident history and market changes; benchmark accuracy cannot establish resale valuation accuracy.
conclusion: Measured results: MAE = 0.6152; RMSE = 0.7668; R2 = 0.9389; baseline_MAE = 2.5203. The generated price rule omits brand, condition, accident history and market changes; benchmark accuracy cannot establish resale valuation accuracy.

title: Credit Card Fraud Detection
aim: Detect unusual transactions from numerical features using an unsupervised anomaly detector.
data: 2,000 generated transactions: 1,940 normal and 60 anomalies. Labels are used only for stratification and final evaluation, not model fitting.
theory: Isolation Forest isolates observations using random partitions; anomalies tend to require shorter paths. The contamination rate is fixed in advance at 3 percent, not tuned on held-out labels.
code:
normal = rng.normal(0, 1, size=(1940, 5))
anomalies = rng.normal(2.8, 1.5, size=(60, 5))
X = pd.DataFrame(np.vstack([normal, anomalies]), columns=[
    'log_amount_z', 'distance_z', 'velocity_z', 'hour_risk_z', 'device_risk_z'])
y = np.r_[np.zeros(len(normal), dtype=int), np.ones(len(anomalies), dtype=int)]
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25,
                                    stratify=y, random_state=SEED)
model = IsolationForest(n_estimators=200, contamination=0.03,
                        random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1)
model.fit(Xtr)  # No labels supplied to the unsupervised estimator.
pred = (model.predict(Xte) == -1).astype(int)
risk = -model.decision_function(Xte)
print(f'Train: {len(Xtr)} | Test: {len(Xte)} | Test anomalies: {sum(yte)}')
print('Labels: 0 = normal; 1 = anomaly')
print(classification_report(yte, pred, digits=3, zero_division=0))
metrics = {'average_precision': average_precision_score(yte, risk),
           'anomaly_f1': f1_score(yte, pred),
           'prevalence_baseline_AP': float(yte.mean())}
for key, value in metrics.items(): print(f'{key}: {value:.4f}')
ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(yte, pred, cmap='Blues', colorbar=False)
plt.title('Held-out anomaly detection')
plot_save('10_fraud_detection')
limitation: An anomaly is not proof of fraud. The generated anomalies are deliberately separated, making this easier than most real transaction datasets.

title: Student Performance Prediction
aim: Predict a final academic score from attendance, study hours, assignments, previous scores and participation.
data: 900 generated students. Marks and attendance are percentages; study hours are weekly. The regression option allowed by the assignment is used.
theory: Gradient boosting fits successive shallow trees to reduce the residual error of an additive model. Learning rate and tree complexity control model capacity.
code:
n = 900
X = pd.DataFrame({'attendance': rng.uniform(40, 100, n),
    'study_hours': rng.uniform(0, 30, n),
    'assignment_marks': rng.uniform(20, 100, n),

     + 0.3*X.previous_scores + 0.8*X.participation
     + rng.normal(0, 5, n)).clip(0, 100)
model = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=150, learning_rate=0.05,
                                  max_depth=2, random_state=SEED)
metrics = evaluate(model, X, y, '11_student_performance', classification=False)
limitation: Predictive associations in synthetic records are not causal explanations of student achievement.
conclusion: Measured results: MAE = 4.5706; RMSE = 5.7228; R2 = 0.8144; baseline_MAE = 10.8046. Predictive associations in synthetic records are not causal explanations of student achievement.

title: Dimensionality Reduction of Handwritten Digits
aim: Reduce handwritten-digit image features while retaining information and visualize samples in two dimensions.
data: scikit-learn Digits benchmark: 1,797 images, each 8 x 8 pixels with intensities from 0 to 16.
theory: PCA finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance. A 95-percent-variance representation is compared with a separate two-component visualization. PCA is fitted only on training images; labels are used only to colour the held-out plot.
code:
dataset = load_digits()
X, y = dataset.data / 16.0, dataset.target
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25,
                                    stratify=y, random_state=SEED)
pca95 = PCA(n_components=0.95, svd_solver='full').fit(Xtr)
compressed = pca95.transform(Xte)
reconstructed = pca95.inverse_transform(compressed)
pca2 = PCA(n_components=2, svd_solver='full').fit(Xtr)
points = pca2.transform(Xte)
metrics = {'components_for_95pct': pca95.n_components_,
    'retained_variance': pca95.explained_variance_ratio_.sum(),
    'two_dimensional_variance': pca2.explained_variance_ratio_.sum(),
    'test_reconstruction_MSE': mean_squared_error(Xte, reconstructed)}
print(f'Train: {len(Xtr)} | Test: {len(Xte)} | Original features: 64')
for key, value in metrics.items(): print(f'{key}: {value:.4f}')
plt.scatter(points[:, 0], points[:, 1], c=yte, cmap='tab10', s=15, alpha=0.8)
plt.colorbar(ticks=range(10), label='True digit (visualization only)')
plt.xlabel('Principal component 1'); plt.ylabel('Principal component 2')
plt.title('Held-out digits projected into two dimensions')
plot_save('13_digits_pca')
limitation: Two principal components retain much less information than the 95-percent representation; class overlap in two dimensions is expected.

title: Sales Prediction
aim: Predict future sales from advertising, previous sales, product price, discounts and seasonal features.
data: 600 generated daily observations; sales are units, advertising and price are currency units, discount is a fraction. The final 150 days form the test period.
theory: AdaBoost combines weak regression trees while increasing attention to poorly predicted observations. Evaluation uses a chronological split; previous-day sales are observable for rolling one-day-ahead prediction.
code:
n = 601
advertising = rng.uniform(10, 100, n)
price = rng.uniform(15, 40, n)
discount = rng.uniform(0, 0.3, n)
season = np.sin(2*np.pi*np.arange(n)/30)
sales = np.zeros(n); sales[0] = 100
for t in range(1, n):
    sales[t] = max(0, 30 + 0.45*sales[t-1] + 1.2*advertising[t]
        - 1.3*price[t] + 80*discount[t] + 15*season[t]
        + rng.normal(0, 8))
X = pd.DataFrame({'advertising': advertising[1:],
    'previous_sales': sales[:-1], 'price': price[1:],
    'discount': discount[1:], 'seasonal_signal': season[1:]})
y = sales[1:]
model = AdaBoostRegressor(n_estimators=150, learning_rate=0.05,
                          loss='square', random_state=SEED)
metrics = evaluate(model, X, y, '15_sales_prediction',
                   classification=False, chronological=True)
cut = int(len(y)*0.75)
metrics['persistence_MAE'] = mean_absolute_error(y[cut:], X.previous_sales.iloc[cut:])
print(f'Previous-day persistence MAE: {metrics["persistence_MAE"]:.4f}')
limitation: This is rolling one-day-ahead forecasting with known advertising and price. Multi-day forecasting would need predicted lags and a separate evaluation.
